uniequip_002_agoat2:
[Recording: Bubbling lava]
Title: Volcano's Breathing
Description:
When the Mount Siesta stopped erupting, Professor Keller and I climbed up the volcano once again to finish our last data collection.
After we recorded this sound of bubbling lava, Professor Keller suddenly suggested that we sit for a while at the mountaintop.
She gazed at the already ash-grey Siesta and I saw her eyes swell up with tears. She mentioned something about the future of the Volcano Museum of Siesta and her plans for retirement, which would very likely be delayed. I knew that she wanted me to visit Siesta as much as possible in the future—not just for research.

[Recording: Singing with music]
Title: Singing at a Cake Shop
Description:
It's been a while since I last came back, and I had this feeling that this little town was stuck in time and nothing was ever going to change.
However, I accidentally noticed that the cake shop Mom used to like so much had finished its renovation and reopened. A lot of musicians even came to the courtyard, holding impromptu performances.
I heard a very familiar melody that day and went up close, and the singer invited me to join them! *Sighs* It was a pity I couldn't remember the lyrics and wasn't quite sure which part everyone was singing, so I just struggled to hum along... Hope I wasn't off-key too much.

[Recording: An academic talk]
Title: On-campus Seminar
Description:
I brought the data from Mount Siesta back to Wilhelm University and met with Dr. Kahn and other scholars there. Dr. Kahn seemed a little unsettled. I told him it was not a big deal, but by the looks of it, that wasn't much help.
Thankfully, after some small talk, we started discussing research on volcanoes, and Dr. Kahn finally found peace and became more relaxed.
The seminar was exciting. No one seemed to care that we were not in a classroom, laboratory, or meeting room, but just standing on a path on campus.
It felt really nice.

[Recording: Ripped audio from a childhood video]
Title: I Still Remember That Wish
Description:
I left the university and came back home.
I changed the curtains, threw away some old stuff I didn't need anymore, and found a childhood video in the process. It was a shame that most of the content was damaged. Fortunately, the soundtracks were intact, so I got to rip them and re-record them onto this tape.
I heard Mom and Dad singing me the birthday song and encouraging me to make a wish. Of course, I didn't say it out loud, but I still remember it—
Now I'm on my way to making it come true.

[Recording: Friends' laughing]
Title: A Welcome Party For Me!
Description:
I returned aboard for my regular check-up after settling everything at home. It'd been a long time since I last left Rhodes Island, and guess what? People held a welcome party for me!
Provence and Angelina caused a little chaos when they set off the firework tubes and accidentally knocked down a huge pile of dolls. Then next thing I remember was little lambs coming from nowhere and rampaging all about... It was a disaster. But everyone was laughing so hard.
I really hope these kinds of moments can last longer.

[Recording: N/A]
Title: Untitled
Description:
For the next field investigation.
I'd love to keep more recordings if I have the chance—the sound of lava, wind, rain, and the people around me.
uniequip_003_agoat2:
[Designation] 'Marshmallow' No. 3
[Description] A mutant of the Volcano Watcher obtained through radiation-induced mutagenesis; its traits have become largely stable after four generations of selective breeding. While retaining the favorable traits of the parent variety, it has acquired an early-flowering phenotype and can be transplanted even during the flowering period. Should Originium activity in the soil environment exceed a certain threshold, a color-change reaction can be rapidly observed at the cut surface of the stem, allowing a precursor of volcanic eruption to be identified faster than by the original method of reading petal coloration.
[Cultivation Management] In order to maintain sample numbers, preserve the purity of the variety, and avoid divorcing it from its actual environment, the research group has adopted living cultivation for the conservation of the germplasm of 'Marshmallow' No. 3. With the support of the College of Geology at Wilhelm University in Leithanien and Rhodes Island's New Siesta office, its day-to-day cultivation management has already been handed over to dedicated personnel; regular inspections are nevertheless required to ensure that propagation and conservation cultivation proceed smoothly. For precautions, see the appendix.
[Addendum] Since last month, staff on duty have reported that the plants are frequently gnawed at by unidentified creatures, yet a review of the surveillance footage turned up nothing at all. After Miss Naumann hurried to the site to investigate, she offered the following suggestions and reminders for the reference of the personnel concerned:
1. Each day, set out fresh grass, fruit, and ice cream on the newly installed table. The varieties of fruit and ice cream must be changed daily, and ideally should not repeat within the same week;
2. The television in the break room is best left switched on at all times; furthermore, playing the eight o'clock morning program 'Siesta Traffic Report,' the noon program 'Volcano Kitchen, Teen Edition,' and the eight o'clock evening program 'Love in Siesta' season thirteen on schedule can effectively reduce the rate of damage to the plants (this program list will be updated periodically);
3. Please take stock of your personal belongings each day. If anything has gone missing, you may set an extra marshmallow on the table the following day and check your own pockets the day after; should you find an item of unknown origin among them, please report it and hand it in.
To the staff who still harbored doubts, Miss Naumann left these words—
'Don't worry, they mean no harm—they're only a little curious. Sometimes I find myself thinking... when a volcano erupts and the lava comes rushing down along the ranges, it is as though the earth were baring its veins. At times like that I feel I can almost hear an enormous heart beating deep underground, wanting to say something, only we cannot understand it yet. Perhaps they are waiting for the same thing we are—for these flowers, bred generation after generation, to transform into some new shape and read the words of the earth for us.'
